content: The number of individuals eligible for antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be determined using data from programmatic sources, surveillance systems (including case-based surveillance), and surveys. These data should be disaggregated by sex, age, key populations, and geographic location. The Spectrum AIDS Impact Model (AIM) can be utilized to address data gaps, as it incorporates country-specific demographic data, such as population size, structure, fertility, mortality, and migration rates, to produce national estimates. Users can input additional data, including the number of individuals receiving ART and prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) care, as well as HIV surveillance and survey data that describe prevalence levels and trends. In countries with robust HIV reporting and vital registration systems, HIV case data and AIDS-specific mortality data may also be used to refine estimates. The Spectrum AIM model integrates assumptions about disease progression and the distribution of HIV incidence by sex and age. These assumptions can be adjusted if more accurate country-specific data are available. The model combines these inputs and assumptions to generate various impact indicators commonly used to monitor the HIV epidemic, such as the number of people living with HIV, new infections, AIDS-related deaths, ART coverage, and PMTCT coverage. For adults (ages 15+), the model uses HIV prevalence data from national surveillance systems to estimate the trajectory of the epidemic over time. In countries with high-quality data, HIV case and AIDS-specific mortality data may also inform incidence estimates. Annual HIV incidence is calculated based on prevalence and the number of individuals receiving ART. Assumptions about demographic structure, disease progression (e.g., CD4 count at diagnosis), and survival rates for those on and off ART are applied to estimate the number of adults living with HIV each year. The outputs provide disaggregated data by age, sex, pregnancy status, geographic area, and key populations. For children (ages <15), the model estimates the number of births to HIV-infected mothers based on adult HIV prevalence. It calculates the annual number of children infected through mother-to-child transmission during pregnancy, delivery, or breastfeeding. Assumptions about the survival of HIV-infected children, based on time since infection, diagnosis, and ART coverage, are applied to estimate the number of children living with HIV annually. The outputs are disaggregated by age and sex. The estimated number of people living with HIV is the sum of infected adults and children. ART eligibility is estimated by considering the proportion of the population eligible based on CD4 count or other criteria (e.g., age, pregnancy, TB co-infection, serodiscordant couples, hepatitis B/C). Countries can modify these values if more accurate data are available. ART eligibility for children can be specified by CD4 count, percentage, or age. The model compares the estimated number of people living with HIV, disaggregated by CD4 count and other factors, with national treatment guidelines to estimate the number of newly eligible individuals for ART. This figure is added to the number of individuals already receiving ART to estimate the total eligible population. The number of pregnant women eligible for PMTCT is estimated by multiplying the number of HIV-positive women in each five-year age group (15–49) by age-specific fertility rates, adjusted for differences in fertility between HIV-positive and HIV-negative women. Fertility adjustments are based on default values but can be modified with country-specific data. Stigma and discrimination remain significant barriers to effective HIV prevention, care, and treatment. These issues disproportionately affect key populations at higher risk of HIV, such as sex workers, men who have sex with men, and people who inject drugs, as well as all individuals living with HIV. Stigma and discrimination by healthcare providers discourage individuals from seeking testing, adopting preventive behaviors, and enrolling in care and treatment services. These behaviors may stem from inadequate training, lack of knowledge, or fear of HIV. Stigma is a societal judgment often rooted in ignorance or false beliefs, while discrimination involves actions that deny individuals or communities their rights. Protection against discrimination is a recognized international human right, and many countries have enshrined non-discrimination against people living with HIV in their constitutions or legislation. Documenting the prevalence of stigma and discrimination in the general population and among healthcare providers helps identify training and policy needs to address these barriers. Data can be collected through representative surveys of key populations and the general population, as well as exit interviews at healthcare facilities. The Stigma Index, developed by the Global Network of People Living with HIV/AIDS (GNP+), UNAIDS, and other organizations, provides insights into stigma through surveys of people living with HIV. Since 2008, over 50 countries have completed the study, training more than 1,300 individuals living with HIV to conduct surveys and interviewing over 50,000 participants. The delivery of HIV prevention, care, and treatment services depends on the capacity of the underlying health system. The World Health Organization (WHO) has identified six building blocks of functional health services: service delivery infrastructure, the health workforce, medical products and technology, financing, information, and leadership and governance. Deficiencies in any of these components can compromise the system's ability to deliver HIV services. Programmatic monitoring should track service availability, readiness, quality, and oversight, as well as linkages between services.
